1:
The date is the first difficulty and everyone stops at it, since the young man had been three years in training and is here already numbered with the wise men. Gill lists the Jewish answers — the second year after the temple fell, the second of the monarchy once the surrounding nations were subdued, the second after the Egyptians were beaten, and one rabbi's reckoning of the second year counting back from the end of the reign, which even his own commentators called an unusual way of counting — and rejects them all as too late, since the man was famous for wisdom long before. Henry suggests he may have been forward enough to be taken into service after one year rather than three, or that the second year is counted from the day he first stood before the king, as an earlier interpreter of dreams rose in the second year after his own skill appeared. Wesley takes that line flatly: properly the fifth year of the reign, but the second after Daniel was brought in. Clarke and Calvin prefer the co-regency, the first two years having been shared with his father, and Ellicott notes the king had already been called king of Babylon by anticipation while his father lived.

Four classes are summoned and the philologists divide them. Keil and Delitzsch derive the first from the word for a stylus, making them men who went about with the pen, learned in the sacred writings; the second from a root meaning to breathe or whisper, since they worked their incantations by movements of the breath; the third are the magicians found also in Egypt and, on a prophet's testimony, a powerful body in Babylon; the fourth are the Chaldean priestly caste. Ellicott follows the same derivations but doubts the last are a separate class at all, taking them for the priests and counting them inside the first. Clarke confesses the Chaldeans are hard to identify and guesses at a college where all the arts were professed and taught, the name being kept exclusively by one people among the hundred and twenty provinces. Wesley says the magicians assumed the national name as the most noble.

Both Gill and Ellicott note that the plural dreams gives way at once to the singular: it was one dream containing various parts, and Wesley says the same.

Whether the king had actually forgotten it is the real dispute. Clarke has nothing left in the morning but the uneasy impression. Gill, Wesley and Ellicott hold he remembered in general but could not repeat it, Ellicott putting it that he retained a portion and lost the outline. Keil and Delitzsch deny he had forgotten at all, allowing only an oppressive recollection that he had dreamed; they cite the king's own later words, that if the wise men cannot declare the dream they have agreed to speak deceitfully, and they raise the stake by naming critics who use the forgetting to call the whole story unhistorical, the demand madness and the rage unmotivated. Gill reports a rabbi who went the other way entirely, that the king knew his dream perfectly and was testing them; Ellicott thinks the Chaldeans' behaviour makes that possible, though he does not adopt it.

Calvin reads the sleeplessness as evidence of the dream's author. This was not the king's first dream, but the terror impressed on his mind would not let him rest, like a sting that kept him troubled until he had the meaning; and Calvin allows that even profane writers rightly connected dreams with divine agency, while warning it would be foolish to extend this to every dream, since dreams also rise from the day's thoughts and men who read a conjecture into each one make themselves ridiculous.
4:
The book changes language here and all of them mark it. Gill and Clarke say the Chaldee runs from here to the end of the seventh chapter, Wesley the same in other words; Gill explains the choice as the mother tongue of both parties, easier to speak and to be understood. Ellicott suspects the notice was a heading telling a copyist where the Aramaic begins, dismisses the conjecture that this portion translates a lost Hebrew original, and supplies a reason of his own: what is to be revealed concerns the Gentile world, so a Gentile language carries it. Keil and Delitzsch caution that nothing follows from the notice about what language the king himself spoke. On the salutation Clarke reaches for a modern parallel, that in the East a superior still blesses an inferior with long life to thee, and a poor petitioner uses the same words to a king.

What the king means by saying the thing is gone from him is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch set out the case: two ancient versions treat the word as a verb of departing, which yields that the dream has escaped him, while others take it otherwise. Ellicott decides for the second sense, that the order has been published and cannot be recalled. Calvin allows both and inclines to the vanished dream, since the expression returns a few verses later where the dream seems meant.

Threat and bribe come together. Clarke calls the sentence arbitrary and tyrannical in the extreme, while noting providence overruled it to a purpose; Ellicott answers that the punishment was by no means uncommon, and points to Assyrian evidence. Calvin thinks the demand itself unjust, since the wise men professed to interpret dreams and never to recover them, so the king ignores the limits of their art. On the promised rewards Calvin observes what all history declares, that the Magi made a trade of their predictions, and sets against them the wise men of the Indies, frugal and austere, who needed neither money nor furniture.

The defence is heard differently. Keil and Delitzsch say the Chaldeans concealed a confession of ignorance under the claim that the thing was beyond human power. Ellicott calls their appeal to precedent a delicate flattery and exposes the reasoning: no king ever left a precedent for such a request, therefore the request is impossible. Calvin thinks the excuse just in itself, though the king would not admit it, and reads the episode as arranged to prove the Magi impostors. Clarke turns their verdict into evidence, since their own judgment that no man on earth could do it made the young Hebrew's success decisive by their own theology. Ellicott explains the charge about changing times as an accusation of stalling for a luckier day, Eastern notions of fortunate days being what the king suspects.

The clause about gods who do not dwell with flesh divides the commentators sharply. Ellicott finds behind it a doctrine of Babylonian religion in which every man had a deity attached from birth who lived in him and so shared human infirmity, open to evil spirits and even capable of injuring the person it guarded; not even those gods, the wise men urge, could do this. Keil and Delitzsch deny any distinction of higher and lower gods is present, and read only the plain difference between gods and men, flesh standing against spirit as the mark of mortal weakness.

How far the decree reached is a last question. Keil and Delitzsch insist it was never fully carried out, the participle meaning the killing had merely begun. Gill notes some versions read it as done, and supposes those at court were killed while officers went out for the rest. Ellicott limits it to wise men resident in Babylon, and notes the young Hebrew had been trained but never appointed, so his danger came only from the general order.
14:
Two of them ask why the man the king had judged ten times wiser was never sent for. Henry answers that everything was done in a heat and nothing with deliberate thought, but providence so ordered it, since the magicians being nonplussed first meant the more glory afterwards; meanwhile an undiscriminating sentence condemns him and he knows nothing until notice arrives. Calvin calls it the king's sloth, since he should have recalled the incredible gift of heavenly wisdom already seen among the captives of Judah, and adds that God was unwilling his servant should mix with ministers of Satan whose whole knowledge was juggling and error; tyrants are unjust, he says, because they will not undertake the labour of inquiry.

The captain's office is read two ways. Gill offers the guard, the militia, the cooks or the executioners; Clarke settles on the last and makes it chief of the butchers, the man who took heads off at the king's displeasure, citing the courtier who fetched a head in a bag on a dish and the officer who carried a prophet's head to a dancing girl, and concluding that with no law, no judge and no jury the king's caprice governs all. Keil and Delitzsch make it chief of the bodyguard, the highest office in the kingdom, whose business was to see the king's commands executed; on the man's name they reject a derivation from a Sanskrit word for venerable and prefer a formation from the word for a lion. Henry and Clarke both break off into the same aside, congratulating their countrymen on living under law rather than a prince's caprice.

Gill notes the first verb has been read as inquiring after the law and decree and also as causing the decree to be returned, that is, staying the execution, and prefers the first; Keil and Delitzsch render it that he answered words of counsel and understanding. On the question about haste, Ellicott says Daniel meant Arioch to understand the thing was not impossible after all, and Keil and Delitzsch agree while correcting a rendering that would turn the participle into a predicate and give why is the command so hostile. Calvin hears an oblique reproach, an expostulation that he was neither called nor listened to and yet was to die for the failure of others.

Going in was bold on both sides. Gill observes that Arioch suspended his orders and Daniel walked into a furious king's presence carrying the name of a wise man, and credits the providence that moved both. Ellicott draws two marks of the man who trusts God rather than his learning: courage, to venture in on a humane errand, and humility, to ask for time, where the wise men had called the thing impossible and never asked an extension; he adds that we are nowhere told the time was granted, or that more than an interpretation was promised, many scriptural narratives being very condensed. Clarke marks the contrast differently: the Chaldeans would not promise so much, pledging only an interpretation if the dream were supplied, while Daniel undertakes to recover the dream as well. Calvin thinks the prefect was not without fear, being in danger for the delay, and reads it as God bending and taming his mind.

Gill places the house near the palace and rejects a traveller's report setting it twenty miles off, since the orders reached only the wise men of Babylon and Daniel was found among them. On the title used in the prayer, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree it appears once in the patriarchal history but came into common use only during the exile, as the name of the true God set against the gods of the heathen. Calvin notices that the man who already had the gift, and who alone of the four was a prophet, still calls the other three to implore mercy with him.
19:
Whether the revelation came as a dream is disputed. Gill reports the view that it did, and that Daniel dreamed the king's own dream and remembered what the king forgot, though he leaves open whether the image was shown him sleeping or waking. Clarke keeps the same two options and chooses neither. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the identification: a night vision need not be a dream, Daniel does not call it one, and such a vision is simply one received at night while a man is awake. They add that the notion of an identical dream was imported by a critic who wanted a psychological impossibility to discredit the narrative with. Ellicott agrees it was literally a vision and says a repetition of the king's dream cannot be inferred, though both kinds of revelation are provided for elsewhere.

Calvin takes the answered prayer as evidence about the praying. Since God showed himself propitious, the man cannot have wavered, for one driven about like a wave is told he shall receive nothing; persuaded that his life was in God's hands and that the king's mind had not been troubled for nothing, he prayed as though he had already obtained his request.

On the thanksgiving Keil and Delitzsch note the verb keeps its proper force, the revelation being an address from God and this the answer to it. Ellicott finds the doxology built on an existing liturgical form, the one closing a psalm and taken up later at a public reading of the law, and observes the prayer is largely framed on scriptural language while fitted to a new need. Calvin explains the vehemence: a man snatched from death beyond expectation is the more stirred to praise, as elsewhere a new song is said to be put into the mouth.

The changing of times and seasons is where they exert themselves. Keil and Delitzsch would reverse the Greek order of the two words and distinguish them as the general circumstance of time and the measured point of time, the pairing making the point that all revolutions whatever hang on the will of God. Ellicott draws the same contrast between circumstances and epochs and ties it to the dream just given, where the changes of future times were so marvellously depicted. Gill runs the range from day and night and summer and winter to the revolutions of states, naming the dream's four monarchies. Clarke says duration and succession are God's, and because his providence puts down one king and raises another he can tell beforehand what he has purposed for the empires of the earth. Wesley sets it against the alternatives: what the heathen ascribed to nature or chance is here ascribed to God.

Ellicott alone works at the clause about light, suggesting illumination rather than light is the meaning, since man needs illuminating from a source outside him, and that source is God, in whom light dwells as though he were a palace. Calvin presses the giving of wisdom further than the previous line: not only has every man his measure of ordinary prudence, enough to tell justice from injustice and order his life, but God adorns some with an understanding so unusual that they appear as his interpreters, which is the gift of prophecy.

On the God of the fathers Gill names the patriarchs and the promises made to them. Ellicott notices the wisdom acknowledged is not the interpretation but the earlier learning, so the man treats his proficiency in Chaldean studies and his skill with dreams as alike supernatural. Calvin uses the phrase to set the God of Israel against the multitude of invented deities, then guards it against misuse: the glory is not founded on ancestral authority, as with those who count the ages an error has prevailed and take the consent of mankind for an oracle, nothing being vainer than men's minds.
24:
Gill notes he went the moment the secret was given, though not before giving thanks; then he spent the answer on his rivals. Henry allows some deserved death as magicians by God's law, but insists what they stood condemned for was no crime worth dying for, so let them live and be justly shamed; since God shows common kindness to evil and good, we should be ready to save even bad men's lives, a good man being a common good, as a ship's company was once given to one prisoner. Ellicott calls it humanity toward his heathen teachers and notes the decree was stopped by that intercession alone; Clarke has it merely suspended pending the trial. Calvin raises the obvious objection, that magical arts ought rather to be abolished outright, being diabolical, and answers that the corruptions were many but the principles sound, so he would not condemn the whole; he doubts too the interpreters who find magic simply condemned here, and infers from the delay that some Magi were already dead.

Getting to the king needed a channel. Ellicott supposes Babylonian custom allowed only chief officers direct access, as the Persian and Median did, so the earlier approach must have gone through the captain too; and it was not strictly true that he had searched for an interpreter. Calvin agrees the request for time went through him, those kings counting courtesy a profanation of their majesty, and adds that the captain's speech shows how courtiers dress up their own good offices.

The parenthesis about the name is doing work. Keil and Delitzsch take it to mean the king knew no Daniel, only the Chaldean name given by the conqueror. Ellicott reads it as a reminder to the reader and denies the king was ignorant of the man, having lately examined him; what surprises him is that where the experienced failed, a novice should succeed. Wesley thinks the king took courage from the name he had bestowed, which means keeper of secret treasure. Calvin hears despair in the question, the king having thought the Magi alone possessed wisdom, and finds it drawn out of a proud man so the grace should show brighter.

The list of practitioners defeats them all. Clarke notes the last name renders an old English word for tellers of truth but belongs to another class, perhaps men who divined by numbers or amulets. Calvin declines the question, since the Jews themselves can only guess, bold in definition and rash in affirmation while unable to distinguish the sorts. Clarke adds that asking whether the king's own men, aided by his gods, could tell him was necessary, so he might see the folly of trusting one and worshipping the other. Ellicott says the reply concedes the wise men's case: what they claimed was true, since the gods who dwell with flesh could not reveal this, and all power of prediction is denied to heathen gods. Gill hears in the answer an assertion of one God against the many, revelation belonging to him alone.

On what is being predicted they part. Clarke says the phrase about the latter days generally means, in the prophets, the Messiah's times. Ellicott takes the corresponding word to mean simply hereafter, in the course of history, and not the Messianic days only. Ellicott observes that the visions of the head are called thoughts because thinking was the natural channel of a supernatural message: they came unforced while the king's mind was on further conquests. Wesley admires the approach: the prophet does not fall abruptly on the dream but prepares a lofty king by degrees, to win him to the true God. The disclaimer is decisive: the secret came for the king's sake and by no wisdom of the speaker's own, since, as Calvin puts it, a man might surpass the world in intelligence and still never divine what another had dreamt.
31:
Henry begins with the transaction. The king had paid for this man's maintenance and education and preferred him at court, and is now repaid; having received a prophet, though not in the name of a prophet, he gets a prophet's reward, of a kind only a prophet could give. Then Henry turns the image against its dreamer. Here is a worshipper of images, likely an admirer of statues who had adorned his palace with them, and a great image is now set before him in a dream, which might have taught him what the things he spent so much upon really were: he could shut his eyes, represent to himself what forms he pleased and beautify them at will, without the expense or trouble of sculpture.

Ellicott insists on a word in the text: it is properly one great image, and the oneness is the point. Though many members are named, only four parts answer to the four metals, so the history of the world in its bearing on God's people, complicated as it looks, consists of no more than four principal divisions; the further detail given later marks minor complications that do not disturb the fourfold outline.

The metals are assigned with little dispute. Clarke runs them off in order: the head Babylonian, the breast and arms Medo-Persian, the belly and thighs Macedonian, the legs Roman, and the feet that same empire mixed with barbarian nations and divided into ten kingdoms. Gill gives the head fine gold for its glory, excellence and duration, and takes the iron for a coarser metal that is yet very strong; he alone reads the two legs as the eastern and western empires into which the Roman was later divided. Calvin says all writers of sound judgment understand the four monarchies without controversy, and charges those who confuse the Turkish empire with the Roman with an ignorance easily proved, since what they are avoiding is the confession that Christ was exhibited to the world.

Keil and Delitzsch work through the anatomy instead, fixing the opening construction as a phrase about the image rather than a sentence, tracing the words for breast, for the belly enclosing the bowels, for the thighs and upper loins, and for the leg including the upper thigh, and noting the clause about the feet is partitive.

On the stone the readings converge and then divide again. Gill takes it for the Messiah and marshals support, that Jewish writers ancient and modern read it so as well as Christians, one old book identifying it with the Shepherd and Stone of Israel and another making the ninth of ten kings the King Messiah. Clarke calls it a fifth monarchy, the spiritual kingdom which lasts for ever and spreads over the whole earth, and distinguishes the kingdom of the stone from that of the mountain. Calvin raises the difficulty himself: if Christ is the wisdom by whom kings reign, how should his coming break up an order God approves and established? His answer is that earthly empires are broken only accidentally, since if kings discharged their office honestly his kingdom would not be against their power; it is because their pride is untameable, and they would pull God from his throne if they could, that they must feel his hand against them. Of the Roman fall he observes that no outside force brought it down, which is why he takes it to have been broken by Christ.

Ellicott ends with what the stone did not do: it never struck the head, breast or loins, which became fragments only by falling once the feet were gone. Gill says the same from the other side, that the basis being broken the whole body came down and shattered by its own weight; and Ellicott adds that the chaff of the summer threshing floors is standing language for divine judgment.
36:
Ellicott and Wesley both stop at the plural in we will tell: it takes in the three companions, to whose intercession the revelation was owed, and Wesley reads piety and modesty in it, a refusal to arrogate what four had begged from God.

The title king of kings is disputed on grammatical grounds. Gill reports Jewish interpreters who join it to the next clause and make it a description of God, so that the King of kings who is the God of heaven has given the kingdom; he answers that this runs against the accents. Clarke keeps it of the man and presses the giver: the kingdom came neither from his own gods nor his own prowess, and with it came power to rule, strength to defend and glory for dignity.

Calvin explains why the list starts where it does. The Assyrians had been subdued before the monarchy passed to Babylon, but never prevailed enough to count as supreme, and God was not concerned with what had already happened; the point was that the people should have something to lean on in future, the Chaldeans having sixty or seventy years still to run. Wesley gives the reason for the gold as the vast riches of that monarchy, and that it stood longest, five hundred years, flourishing to the last.

In what sense the second kingdom is inferior nobody agrees. Ellicott locates it in the divided character of the empire against the massive solidity of its predecessor, shown by the two breasts answering to the one head as well as by the poorer metal, and grants that in territory and duration it far exceeded the Babylonian. Calvin denies inferiority of power or wealth altogether, the Chaldean empire being simply added to that of the Medes and Persians, and puts it instead in the general condition of the world being worse. Wesley makes it inferior in time, lasting less than half as long. Gill agrees it began as large and as rich, finding the decline in later reigns, down to the Darius who lost it.

Of the third, Keil and Delitzsch note that only here is it said to rule the whole earth, so in extent and power it surpasses what came before; Wesley says brass because coarser, and recalls that its king marched to the Indies and was said to have conquered the world. The fourth is treated at much greater length, as Ellicott observes, and where the second and third each borrowed from the empire before, the Roman crushes out what remains of them and brings in a new system and civilisation. Gill rules out two candidates: not Alexander's successors, who belong to the thighs and in whose time no kingdom of Christ arose, and not the Turkish empire, as three Jewish commentators held. Calvin reaches the same result by tracing what became of Alexander's successors: one yielded his kingdom to the free cities, another was driven beyond the mountains, Macedonia became a province, Egypt was seized.

The mixture is where the fourth kingdom's character shows. Keil and Delitzsch make iron firmness and clay brittleness, and read the mingling as an attempt to bind two materials that will not combine. Ellicott says the outward character remains the strength of iron despite the inward divisions, marked by two legs, then two feet, then ten toes, but the strength is only apparent, discordant elements being present which cannot cohere. Wesley traces the division to civil wars and to provinces throwing off the yoke; Gill identifies the ten toes with the kingdoms into which the western empire broke under the northern invasions, the ten horns elsewhere, some strong like iron and lasting, others of clay and short-lived. On the mingling with the seed of men, Ellicott takes it for the human attempt at union set against what God will do: marriages arranged between the royal houses of the component kingdoms.
44:
Whose days are meant is the first question, and no two answer alike. Ellicott points out that no kings have been mentioned at all up to this point, so they must be the ones the toes stand for; the sense is that while the fourth kingdom still contrives to exist in some modified form, its parts at war and in turmoil, the kingdom of God arrives. Wesley puts it much earlier, while the iron kingdom itself still stood, since the birth fell in the reign of Augustus. Gill will not have any of the first three, nor the old Roman emperors either, but only the ten kings of the divided empire; he traces a beginning under Augustus and Tiberius, growth under Constantine, diminution under the Papacy and revival at the Reformation, but holds the kingdom will not be set up in its glory until the ten have been overcome. Clarke stays with the contrast: every preceding empire was swallowed by the next, and this one alone remains to the end of the world.

Calvin spends the verse arguing with a Jewish commentator who set out six reasons why the fifth kingdom cannot be Christ's, and the exchange is the most substantial thing here. The first objection is that since the four kingdoms were earthly, the fifth must be of the same nature or the comparison is absurd. Calvin answers that Scripture constantly compares the heavenly kingdom with earthly ones, that no comparison requires every point to match, and that some difference between the four and the last is precisely what we should expect.

The second objection is that if religion is what distinguishes kingdoms, then the Babylonian, Persian and Macedonian were all one, since all of them worshipped idols. Calvin replies that religion was never the distinguishing mark: God stripped the Babylonians of power and handed the monarchy to the Medes and Persians, then to the Macedonians, and at last to the Romans, and that is what makes them four.

The third is the hardest. This kingdom was to know no passing away, yet a great part of the world is held by the Turks and religion among Christians is divided, many rejecting the gospel. Calvin's answer is that the objection assumes what he denies, that the kingdom is visible. However scattered and unregarded its subjects, the kingdom stands, since by its own nature it is not outward; the saying that this kingdom is not of this world was meant precisely to remove it from the ordinary forms of government.

The fourth is chronological: if the king in question was born under Augustus, the fourth and fifth monarchies began together, which cannot be. Calvin answers that the rabbi has dated the Roman monarchy from Julius Caesar, whereas it began when Macedon was reduced to a province and the third empire started to decline; unless the fourth is taken to succeed immediately on the passing of the third, nothing in the sequence can follow at all. He adds that the prophecy is not looking at the Caesars in any case, and dismisses as trifling those who make the mingling of races refer to the rivalry of two generals.

The last objection is that once Constantine and his successors professed the faith, the empire and the kingdom cannot be separated, since where Christ is acknowledged as the only King that realm belongs to his. Calvin answers that the prophecy ends the Roman empire at the point where it began to be torn in pieces, and he says elsewhere in the same passage what he thinks that tearing was: no single monarch reigned there but a commonwealth in which all were related and all thought themselves equally kings, a bond which should have made the thing permanent and instead destroyed it, so that the empire perished, against nature, by its own internal discord.
45:
The mountain is new here, and both the closest readers say so. Keil and Delitzsch observe it went unmentioned when the stone was first described and is used deliberately now: a stone must be freed from a mountain before it can roll without a hand, and the mountain can only be Zion, where the God of heaven founded the kingdom that spreads from there over the earth. Ellicott says the same and adds the stone-figure used elsewhere of the Messiah, taking the phrase about hands for the supernatural agency at work.

Ellicott sets the two objects against each other. The image was weak by construction, made of incongruous materials, precious metals at the top and miry clay at the bottom, so the thing was top-heavy; the stone is single, for all the countless particles composing it, and grows in strength as it goes until it becomes a mountain. Wesley finds in the same figure the small beginning of a visible kingdom and an origin unlike any other, a conception without father or mother according to the two natures; and he keeps the double property of the stone, which grinds to powder what it falls on and grows until it fills the earth. Clarke reads the cutting without hands as alluding to the miraculous birth but chiefly to the spiritual nature of a government that used no worldly policy and no military force.

Clarke's long discourse takes positions the others do not. He identifies the legs of iron first with the two kingdoms that came out of Alexander's division, the Egyptian and the Syrian, and only then with the Roman empire which absorbed both; he argues it from the text, since the iron marks not only strength but the violence those houses used against the Jews, and since the marriages arranged between the royal families, far from binding the kingdoms, provoked the bloodiest wars between them. He explains too why the gold, silver and brass break along with the iron and clay though only the feet are struck: the Roman government by then contained the splendour of the Chaldeans, the riches of the Persians, the discipline of the Greeks and the strength of the Egyptian and Syrian houses, with the incoherence of all it had subdued, so that with every political excellence it carried the principles of its own destruction.

He also separates two kingdoms in the figure. The kingdom of the stone smites and breaks until no vestige of the others remains; the kingdom of the mountain fills what has been subdued and governs it in peace. On his reckoning the stone began to strike when the apostles went out pulling down idolatry, and the great blow fell at the conversion of Constantine, when the empire happened to be divided among four emperors at once and was thus an epitome of the four monarchies; the stroke is continual in its effects until idolatry is destroyed everywhere.

Ellicott takes the opposite view of where we stand. The stone is rolling now, he says, as the kingdom of God spreads further every day, but the image is still standing and the stone has not yet fallen on it; only when that moment comes will the kingdoms of the world become the kingdom of the Lord and of his Christ. Where Clarke has the decisive impact in the fourth century and everything since as continuation, Ellicott has the impact still ahead and everything so far as approach.

Keil and Delitzsch close on the two words that end the interpretation, treating the first half of the verse as confirmation of what had just been said to the king. Clarke reads the pair as a claim about the account itself: the dream contains a just representation of things as they shall be, and its parts have been truly explained.
46:
That the prostration was religious, not ceremonial, is agreed on lexical grounds. Keil and Delitzsch grant that falling to the earth is used of honour paid to men, but the second verb only of divine homage; to the king this was a man in whom the gods had manifested themselves, and they set it beside two occasions when an apostle stopped the same thing. Ellicott says the word is always used of adoration offered to an idol, and supposes the king thought the gods dwelt in this man more fully than in his other sages. Gill argues it from the sequel, since the orders that follow rule out civil respect, and a proud monarch would never have gone so far for a captive he took to be a mere man; he was great in spiritual things already, Gill adds, and is now made great in worldly ones. Henry has him treating Daniel as a little god, concluding a divinity was lodged in him.

Whether the act deserves any credit divides them. Clarke says flatly that receiving such worship would have been gross idolatry and it must have been forbidden; Wesley agrees a stop was put to it, though the prostration and the word of command could not be prevented; Gill infers the same from the next verse, where the king has plainly been instructed. Calvin alone gives it half a mark. Given the pride of kings, who scarcely reckon themselves among mortals, there was piety and modesty in this one prostrating himself; and the dream cannot have pleased him, having just heard his own flourishing monarchy pronounced short and certain to perish.

The confession is read three ways. Wesley takes it at full value, the supreme God of all the world, and notes the word for lord carries the sense of high Lord. Ellicott gives much less: the king does not acknowledge this God as the true one, only as worthy of a place in the Babylonian pantheon. Calvin holds both at once. The words are pious and might be taken for proof of real conversion, but profane men are sometimes seized with admiration and will then say everything a true worshipper would, and it lasts no longer than the fit, since they remain wrapped in their superstitions and slip back, as a later episode will show. What he will not give up is the use of it: God meant a heathen king to herald his own power, which profited the Jews who stayed firm while most of their countrymen turned idolaters in captivity.

On the promotion Clarke counts three gifts: the presents, the government of the province, the presidency over the wise men. Keil and Delitzsch work out the offices and note the word for prefect is a foreign term taken into the language. Ellicott admits defeat on the second office, which he says has been inexplicable and awaits further discoveries. Calvin warns ministers that where money is not despised many vices spring up and covetous men traffic in the word, though here the gifts were rightly taken.

The request for the three friends draws one suspicion. Calvin raises it himself, that some ambition might be seen here, and it could be charged as a crime to make a gain of doctrine divinely given; his answer is that the motive was pity for his own people, tyrannically used and everywhere hated. Clarke notes the three had shared the danger and helped by their prayers, and that the influence reached only the one province, not the empire. Ellicott makes them satraps under his supervision and reads the gate as marking his higher rank and admission to the inner palace, as Wesley does. Keil and Delitzsch reject a reading that has him ask to be relieved of the office, since a man wishing to keep the dignity and hand over the duty would have needed no appointment, only permission.
